claims.text: The baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy contains dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries.
Internal lamellar boundaries in the baseline alloy are prone to microcrack initiation during tensile loading.
A minor Nb addition followed by controlled post-casting heat treatment will promote Nb segregation to lamellar interfaces.
Cooling conditions that favor segregation will produce a nanometer-scale, alloying-element-enriched layer at lamellar interfaces.
The alloying-element-enriched interfacial layer will strengthen the lamellar boundaries.
Interfacial segregation of the microalloying element increases interfacial cohesion.
Increased interfacial cohesion reduces local stress concentrations.
Reduced local stress concentrations suppress microcrack initiation at lamellar interfaces.
Controlled interface strengthening allows the alloy to retain a refined lamellar structure.
The refined lamellar structure contributes to high strength and improved tensile ductility.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the microalloyed alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in ultimate tensile strength.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the microalloyed alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in room-temperature elongation at failure.
The microalloyed alloy will have a lower density of microcracks at lamellar interfaces than the unmodified baseline.
The unmodified conventionally processed baseline has high strength but limited room-temperature ductility because of microcrack initiation at pristine interfaces.
The proposed improvement is expected to apply across typical eutectic compositions under room-temperature tensile conditions.
Microalloying concentrations above an optimal range may cause embrittlement.
